introduction-cattle-pets-and-guardrails.core: Pets are hand-configured servers you nurse back to health; cattle are identical, replaceable instances built from code. At scale you manage cattle with automation (Systems Manager, CloudFormation) and keep the herd safe with guardrails that detect and correct drift (AWS Config, CloudTrail).

first_principles.problem: Hand-tuned servers can't be rebuilt, and nobody knows who changed what.

analogy.title: A farm with fences and ear tags
analogy.story: Animals are tracked by tag, fences keep them safe, and sick ones are replaced rather than nursed for months.
analogy.breaks: Animals aren't clones; cloud instances from one image are identical.

example.title: Replacing a broken server
flow: Pet: SSH in, debug for hours
Cattle: terminate; ASG launches a fresh one from the template
Root cause investigated from logs later

check.q: What's the key operational benefit of 'cattle' infrastructure?
check.a: Broken instances are replaced from code quickly instead of being repaired by hand.

systems-manager-the-end-of-the-bastion-h.core: Systems Manager's agent lets you manage instances without SSH keys, open ports or bastions. Session Manager gives audited shell access via IAM, Run Command executes scripts across fleets, Patch Manager automates patching, Parameter Store holds config and secrets, and Automation runs runbooks.

first_principles.problem: A bastion host with shared SSH keys is a security risk and nobody audits sessions.
truths: Open SSH ports are attack surface.
derivation: Install the **SSM Agent** and grant the instance role.

analogy.title: A remote control room instead of walking into each machine room
analogy.story: You operate every machine from one console, with every action recorded.
analogy.breaks: Control rooms need wiring; SSM needs the agent and outbound access (or VPC endpoints).

code.text:
aws ssm start-session --target i-0abc123
aws ssm send-command --document-name AWS-RunShellScript \
  --targets Key=tag:role,Values=web --parameters commands='systemctl restart nginx'

check.q: Why is Session Manager more secure than SSH via a bastion?
check.a: No inbound ports or shared keys; access is controlled by IAM and every session is logged.

cloudformation-managing-reality-vs-code.core: CloudFormation turns templates into stacks of resources, computing create/update/delete changes and rolling back on failure. Change sets preview impact, drift detection finds manual changes, stack policies and DeletionPolicy protect critical resources, and StackSets deploy across accounts and regions.

first_principles.problem: Someone edits a security group in the console and the template no longer matches reality.
truths: Code should be the source of truth.

analogy.title: An architect's blueprint versus the actual building
analogy.story: If builders change things without updating the blueprint, the next renovation goes wrong.
analogy.breaks: Buildings can't be rebuilt from blueprints in minutes; stacks can.

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: Replacement=True on the database → stop and rethink.

code.text:
aws cloudformation create-change-set --stack-name db --change-set-name resize \
  --template-body file://db.yaml
aws cloudformation describe-change-set --stack-name db --change-set-name resize \
  --query 'Changes[].ResourceChange.[LogicalResourceId,Action,Replacement]'

check.q: What does a change set show you?
check.a: Which resources will be added, modified or replaced (and whether replacement occurs) before you execute the update.

aws-config-vs-cloudtrail.core: CloudTrail records API calls: who did what, when and from where. Config records resource configuration state and its history, and evaluates it against rules (e.g. 'S3 buckets must block public access'), optionally auto-remediating. Together they answer 'who changed it?' and 'is it compliant now?'.

first_principles.problem: A bucket became public and the team can't tell who did it or whether others are also exposed.
truths: Actions and state are different questions.
derivation: **Org trail** for CloudTrail to a locked S3 bucket.

analogy.title: CCTV versus a building inspector
analogy.story: CCTV shows who walked in and did something; the inspector checks whether the building meets code right now.
analogy.breaks: Inspectors visit occasionally; Config evaluates on every change.

example.title: Public bucket investigation
flow: Config timeline shows policy change at 14:02
CloudTrail: PutBucketPolicy by role dev-admin from IP x

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Who, what, and fixed in minutes.

check.q: Which service tells you a resource's configuration history and compliance?
